content: Thai massage is a traditional form of bodywork originating from Thailand, characterized by a combination of stretching techniques and deep tissue massage. In Thailand, it is referred to as nuat phaen boran, which translates to ancient-style massage, or simply nuat phaen thai. The term nuat phaen boran is derived from the Thai words nuat (massage), phaen (manner), and boran (ancient). Thai massage is also known by various other names, including Northern-style Thai massage, Buntautuk style, Old Medicine Hospital Style, Traditional Thai Massage, Traditional Thai Medical Massage, Thai Yoga, Thai Yoga Massage, yoga massage, Thai classical massage, Thai bodywork, passive yoga, or assisted yoga. Although the roots of Thai Ayurveda and traditional medicine trace back to Tibet, China, and India, the practice of nuat phaen boran is predominantly associated with the northern Chiang Mai region of Thailand. Most practitioners of this style have either trained in Chiang Mai or studied under someone who has. The oldest and most renowned institution for learning this art is the Old Medicine School, also known as the Shivago Komarpai School, which is affiliated with the Buntautuk Hospital Massage Program. This program gained popularity among tourists in the late 1980s and 1990s as a place to learn Thai massage. The founder of the Old Medicine School was the esteemed Grand Master of Traditional Thai Ayurvedic Medicine, Aachan Sintorn Chaichgun. He conducted daily classes for over 30 years until his passing in 2005. His family, including his elder sons Suthat and Wasson, continues to uphold his legacy. Aachan Sintorn was trained in the Wat Po system during the 1950s. The Old Medicine School was a pioneer in offering a simplified 10-day program called Nuat Boran, designed to be accessible to non-Thai speakers. This course focused primarily on technique, with minimal emphasis on theoretical aspects due to language barriers. Unfortunately, many non-Thai learners mistakenly believed that this short program encompassed the entirety of traditional Thai medicine. In reality, becoming a traditional expert or doctor of Thai massage requires approximately two years of full-time hands-on training. Nevertheless, the basic form of Nuat Boran serves as a representative and effective introduction to this unique healing modality. There are between 7 to 10 regional variations of Thai massage, each with its own distinct traditions. These schools often compete for students and recognition, although the Royal Thai Government is currently working to establish common standards and parity among them. During a Thai massage session, the recipient is guided into yoga-like positions while the practitioner applies rhythmic pressure using their hands, forearms, and sometimes feet. The massage often follows the Sen energy lines of the body, which are comparable to the meridians in Chinese medicine. In some techniques, the practitioner uses their legs and feet to stabilize the recipient's body or limbs, while in others, the hands are used for fixation, and the feet perform the massage. Typically, no oil is used, although a hot herbal compress may be applied to warm and soothe the recipient's body. Techniques may include cracking knuckles, walking on the recipient's back, or arching the back in a rolling motion. The massage is performed with a standard procedure and rhythm, and in group settings, practitioners may work in unison. The cost of a Thai massage varies depending on the location, with prices ranging from $5 to $14 USD in 2007, though it can be significantly more expensive in luxury settings such as five-star hotels.
